title: MCP Configuration, Authentication & Secrets
scopeHtml: Scope: MCP server scope and permissions, authentication patterns by service type, secret storage and rotation, and what regulated customers add.

notes.title: MCP scopes and permissions
notes.html:
What an MCP server is, again, in the Claude Code setting. An MCP server is a separate program that exposes tools (and optionally resources and prompts) to Claude; unlike wiring a tool directly into your application, the tool definitions and execution live in the server. Claude Code talks to it over stdio (a local subprocess) or Streamable HTTP (a remote service).

Configuration scope decides which users and projects load the server. Each scope maps to a different configuration location:

Scope Stores the configuration Who loads it Typical use
Local in your local project config, private to you you, in this project only personal experiment not ready to share; a server needing your own credentials
Project a committed .mcp.json at the repo root everyone who clones the repo shared team server (same service for all teammates)
User your user-level config you, in every project a personal tool you want everywhere
Managed admin-deployed configuration everyone in the organization; users can't change it org-wide deployment; centrally controlled integrations

Permission rules can target a single MCP tool. A tool is identified in a permission rule by its server and tool name, so you can allow get_issue on a GitHub server without allowing every tool it exposes, or deny a destructive tool outright. Combine this with the settings hierarchy (deny beats allow; enterprise deny can't be overridden).

Practical guidance.

  • Share a server through the project scope only when it contains no secrets (credentials must be environment references).
  • Prefer narrow, tool-level allow rules over trusting a whole server.
  • Remember that every connected server adds tool definitions to context; connect what you use.
  • For regulated environments, deploy the approved server configuration at managed scope so individual developers can't alter the auth setup.

Real life. A Wi-Fi password: on a sticky note on your own desk (local), on the office wall (project), in your password manager (user), or pushed to every laptop by IT (managed).

Tech. Per-repo, per-user and system-wide git config.

notes.title: Authentication patterns
notes.html:
The right mechanism depends on where the service runs and whose identity it uses.

Service type Pattern How it works
Remote service with user identity (SaaS, cloud services, anything where the user's identity is part of authorization) OAuth The MCP server returns 401 Unauthorized to signal authentication is required; the client starts a browser-based sign-in; after the user approves, a token is issued and stored. No one copies a secret by hand. (The Linear MCP server uses this pattern.)
Remote service with service identity (an internal API identified by a service account) API key via an environment variable The key identifies the service account and must never be committed to configuration; it lives in the environment at the point of execution. In CI using the Agent SDK, the pipeline runner injects it as a secret.
Local service with file-system access stdio, no network authentication The security boundary is the file-system permission model; a deny rule in settings is the governance layer.

The GitHub MCP server is a concrete example of another style: it authenticates with a personal access token passed as a header, with transport and scope chosen by deployment context.

Decision table by deployment context.

Context Transport/scope/auth
Personal local tool (your machine only) stdio, local scope, no network auth
Shared team server Streamable HTTP, project scope (.mcp.json), OAuth or env-var-referenced credentials
Personal experiment local scope, your own credentials
Organization-wide deployment managed scope, admin-controlled
Locked-down governance managed settings, non-overridable

Why enterprise integration differs from a prototype. A prototype answers "does the connection work?". A production integration must also answer: who is the model acting as and is that identity auditable? what data can it access and where does it leave the organization? can an administrator lock the configuration? can access be logged for a compliance audit?

Real life. A hotel: a key card tied to you (OAuth), a staff master key kept in a safe (service key from the environment), and a door that is just physically inside your own house (stdio).

Tech. "Sign in with Google", a service-account key, and a Unix file permission.

notes.title: Secrets
notes.html:
The leak that illustrates it. A developer put an API key inline in a project-scope MCP configuration "to get it working", committed it and pushed. They noticed later, deleted the key from the file and pushed again. The incident is not closed: the key remains in repository history and in every clone. The failure was not a bad auth method; it was a credential that lived in the wrong place and could not be cleaned up once it spread.

Three practices keep a credential from leaking.

  1. Separation. A credential never travels with the configuration that references it. The config holds a variable reference; the value lives somewhere the file doesn't. Config files get committed, shared and cloned, and a value written inline rides along with every copy and enters history in a way overwriting does not remove.
  2. A home for the value. For a value used on one machine or in one pipeline run, an environment variable injected at the point of execution is enough (the CI runner sets it as a secret; the config reads it by name; nothing is written to disk). For a value several services or people need, use a secret store: a managed service that holds credentials, returns them to authorized callers at runtime, and records who read what. It centralizes the value so one rotation updates every consumer and removes the copies each service would otherwise keep in its own files.
  3. Rotation. Replace a credential on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure. Rotation is the only appropriate response to a leaked key, because an exposed key cannot be made secret again. This is why inline credentials are so costly: a value baked into committed code can't be rotated cleanly (the old value stays in history and every consumer hard-coded to it breaks on change). A credential read from the environment or a store rotates without touching the code that uses it, because the code references it by name.

Two cheap habits.

  • Scope each credential to the narrowest access its task needs, so a leak reaches only what that integration required.
  • Keep a record of which services use each credential, so a rotation doesn't surface consumers by breaking them.

Order of response when a key leaks. Revoke/rotate now; replace the inline value with a reference; audit usage logs for the exposure window; add secret scanning (pre-commit/CI) so it doesn't recur. Rewriting git history can help but is never the only fix.

Real life. You lose a house key. Hiding the keyring doesn't help; you change the lock.

Tech. AWS keys pushed to a public repository are scraped within minutes.

notes.title: Regulated integrations
notes.html:
What regulated industries add on top of working authentication. A financial-services or healthcare customer asks more than "does auth work?": where is data processed, how is access logged, can an administrator lock the configuration so a developer can't change the auth setup during an audit window?

Controls and which question each answers.

Customer question Control Why it satisfies it
Can a developer change the auth setup? Enterprise managed configuration An admin-deployed server configuration can't be overridden by individual users; auth is consistent across the organization and doesn't depend on each developer's settings file
Is every access logged? PostToolUse audit hook logging every tool call and its parameters to an audit store The hook fires deterministically for every call regardless of what the model decides, and the log isn't something the model can skip
Where does data go? Region-pinned HTTP endpoint + platform deployment pinned to that region Gives a compliance reviewer a checkable answer; this is why infrastructure requirements and platform choice matter at audit time, not just build time
What can the identity reach? Least-privilege, narrowly scoped credentials Bounded blast radius

Why a prompt isn't a control. Asking Claude to log its actions is a request. User-level settings are editable by each developer. Only deterministic mechanisms (hooks, managed configuration) answer an auditor.

Code modernization example. Applying the full module to legacy change means the auth and integration checklist (identity, secrets, scope, logging, residency) must hold per service type before connecting the agent to legacy systems.

The OAuth that worked in staging and failed in production. A typical review finding: staging used a permissive identity or a locally cached token, production required the full flow with the organization's identity provider and managed configuration; the missing step surfaced only when the configuration moved to production scope. Verify the auth flow end to end in the production-like environment, under the managed settings that will actually apply.

Real life. A bank vault: CCTV the teller can't switch off (hook), keys held by head office (managed config), and the vault physically located in the right country (residency).

Tech. Audit logging at the API gateway rather than trusting each service to log itself.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Scopes. Local (you, this project), project (committed .mcp.json, shared), user (you, all projects), managed (admin; non-overridable). Permission rules can name a single tool by server and tool name.

Authentication. Remote + user identity → OAuth (401 triggers browser sign-in; token stored). Remote + service identity → API key from an environment variable (CI injects as a secret). Local file access → stdio; filesystem permissions are the boundary. GitHub example: personal access token header. Production adds identity auditability, data egress control, admin lock-down and logging.

Secrets. Separation (config holds a reference), a home (env var for one place; secret store for shared), rotation (scheduled and immediately after exposure; baked-in values can't rotate; a committed key stays in history). Narrow scopes; track consumers.

Regulated. Managed config answers "who can change auth?"; PostToolUse audit hook answers "is everything logged?"; region-pinned endpoint + platform answers "where does data go?"; prompts and user settings are not controls.

One-liners.

  • "A leaked key is rotated, not deleted."
  • "Config carries a name; the environment carries the value."
  • "Use deterministic controls for auditors: hooks and managed settings."
  • "OAuth for people, env-var keys for services, filesystem permissions for local."

questions.promptHtml:
A teammate wants an MCP server config shared with everyone who clones the repo. Which scope?

  • A. Local scope
  • B. Project scope (a committed .mcp.json)
  • C. User scope
  • D. Managed scope only

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Project scope writes the server configuration into a file in the repo; local is you in one project; user is you across projects; managed is admin-controlled.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Permission rules can target a single MCP tool by server and tool name, so you can allow get_issue without allowing every tool on the server.

questions.promptHtml:
Match the pattern. A cloud SaaS MCP server where the user's own identity is part of authorization.

  • A. API key in a committed config file
  • B. OAuth: the server returns 401, the client opens a browser sign-in, a token is issued and stored
  • C. stdio with no auth
  • D. A shared password in the system prompt

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. User identity on a remote service → OAuth; service identity on a remote service → API key via environment variable; local filesystem service → stdio where filesystem permissions are the boundary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Remote + user identity → OAuth (401 triggers a browser sign-in; no secret is hand-copied). Remote + service identity → API key injected via environment variable, never committed. Local + file access → stdio, where filesystem permissions are the boundary and a settings deny rule is the governance layer. Committed keys (A) and prompt-embedded passwords (D) are exposures.

questions.contextHtml: A developer put an API key inline in a project-scope MCP config to "get it working", committed it, and pushed. They notice a day later, delete the key from the file and push again.
questions.promptHtml:
Is the incident closed?

  • A. Yes, the key is no longer in the current files
  • B. No: it remains in repository history and in every clone, so rotate it immediately, move the new key to an environment variable or secret store referenced by name, and scope it narrowly
  • C. Yes, if the repo is private
  • D. No, but only a new branch is required

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deleting the line and moving on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who had read access? Was it a service or user credential? What can the key reach?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke and rotate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Exposure through history, forks, CI logs, caches.
  4. How I'd verify each: Audit key usage logs for the exposure window.
  5. Root cause: A value travelled with the configuration that references it.
  6. Fix: Config holds a variable reference; value lives in the environment (CI secret) or a secret manager.
  7. Prevention: Secret scanning pre-commit, narrow scopes, a registry of which services use which credential.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on rewriting history as the only fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Why can't you rotate a baked-in value cleanly? → The old value stays in history and every consumer hard-coded to it breaks on change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes the line.
  • Hire: rotates.
  • Strong hire: rotates, restructures, adds scanning and least privilege.

questions.promptHtml:
An auditor asks for a deterministic record of every tool call and its parameters, plus assurance developers cannot change the auth setup. Which pair of controls answers this?

  • A. A longer CLAUDE.md and a warning comment
  • B. A PostToolUse audit hook (fires regardless of model decisions) and an administrator-deployed managed configuration that users cannot override
  • C. A prompt asking Claude to log its actions
  • D. User-level settings in every laptop

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Hooks are deterministic; managed config is non-overridable; add a region-pinned endpoint to answer "where does data go?".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A PostToolUse hook fires deterministically for every call regardless of what the model decides, so the audit log cannot be skipped. A managed configuration deployed by an administrator cannot be overridden by users, so auth setup is consistent. A prompt (C) is a request, not a control; user-level settings (D) are editable by each developer.

  • A. Project

  • C. User
  • D. Managed

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Local is you in this project; user is you in all projects; project is shared via the repo; managed is admin-controlled.

  • D. It reduces cost
